name: Victor Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Victor, thanks for having me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the foreman at Marsh Lane Farm, which grows cabbages, leeks and onions, and keeps four thousand free-range laying hens. I start at six with the hens, checking the egg belts and the water lines, then I'm out with the picking crew. In winter it's leeks, twelve of us bent over in the mud, and I sort out who's on what row and fix whatever breaks. I like having a crew and getting a field cleared by Friday, and what wears me out is the mud and the phone ringing about orders.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's on the crew, and how do you all talk to each other?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mostly seasonal people from abroad, some have come back for ten years, plus two local lads. A couple of them have very little English, so sometimes I use a translating app on my phone for safety instructions, it's one of the AI ones. I'm not a computer person, but if it works, I use it. Ilona, my wife, works part-time at the pharmacy, and we've still got four years on the mortgage and almost nothing in the bank after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful for some things and that's that. I'd tell the owner it's good we didn't buy anything expensive. I don't really post online, maybe a message in the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. My job is people and mud, and that doesn't change. What I really think about is the mortgage and my knees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. Same crew, same fields, maybe use the app for the rota as well if it helps. I'd spend nothing extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The translation app, would you keep using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because it keeps people safe. Last spring Marek nearly reversed the trailer over Ana's foot, and it was the app that got the word ‘stop’ into Romanian fast enough. Well, I shouted too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next few years look like for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same faces, mostly, maybe fewer of them coming over each year. That's more of a worry than computers: finding enough pickers.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful for some things and that's that, and I'd tell the owner it's good we didn't buy anything expensive. I mostly don't post online.
S0.think: I'd be fine, because my job is people and mud. What I really think about is the mortgage and my knees.
S0.do: Carries on running the crew and fields as normal and might use the translation app for the rota too. Spends nothing extra.
S0.quote: Last spring Marek nearly reversed the trailer over Ana's foot, and it was the app that got the word ‘stop’ into Romanian fast enough.
S0.fieldNote: Victor uses AI only where it proves itself, like the translation app for safety. His real worries are the mortgage, his knees and finding enough pickers. He describes himself as not a computer person but doesn't fear the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen, so we might as well get it right. Farms need picking robots because pickers are hard to find, that's the honest truth. But I'd also say don't drop the people who've come back every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I think picking robots come to vegetables first, and egg collection's already half done by belts. The foreman's job might stay, for a while, minding the machines. But a crew of twelve could become a crew of four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch for a farm nearby that tries a leek harvester robot and I'd go and see it for myself. If it works, I'd ask the owner to send me on the training. And I'd overpay the mortgage a bit every month, even fifty, in case the hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not my job I'm thinking of first, it's whether I can still pay the mortgage if my hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the crew might shrink. Who goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pickers. Ana has done eleven seasons with us, and I'd be the one who tells her not to book the bus next year. I'd hate that more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd wait to see it work elsewhere. What if the owner buys it before you're ready?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd learn on the job, like I learned the egg belts. I'm not quick with new things, but I'm not stupid. I'd ask the dealer for the manual in plain words.

S1.say: I'd say it's going to happen, so let's get it right, because pickers are hard to find. But don't drop the people who've come back every year.
S1.think: Picking robots come to vegetables first, and egg collection is half automatic already. The foreman's job might last a while, but a crew of twelve could become four.
S1.do: Visits a nearby farm trialling a leek-harvesting robot and, if it works, asks the owner for training. Overpays the mortgage by about fifty a month in case his hours drop.
S1.feel: Anxious about the mortgage if his hours drop, more than about his title.
S1.quote: Ana has done eleven seasons with us, and I'd be the one who tells her not to book the bus next year.
S1.fieldNote: Victor's pragmatism shows in accepting that picking robots fill a real labour gap. His sharpest pain is the thought of telling Ana, a picker of eleven seasons, not to come back. He'd learn the machines but wants proof and plain manuals first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to slow it down or at least catch people. I'm not a political man. But a farm can't swap its whole crew in two years and expect the village to be okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of work. If robots can pick leeks and mind hens and fix the egg belt, the owner doesn't need a foreman. And I'd be sixty with four years left on the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank in the first month to talk about the mortgage, before I'm behind, not after. I'd cut everything: the second car, the satellite TV, the trip to see my brother. And I'd look for any job going that a robot isn't doing yet, maybe driving for the council or caretaking at the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be up at night with the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car first, then we'd look at what Ilona's job covers. If it comes down to the house or the car, I'd walk to the farm, it's four kilometres. The house is the thing we'd never give up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd blame for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The owner would just do what everyone else does. Maybe the companies that sell the robots should pay something towards the people they replace, that's fair. But I'm not one to shout.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to slow it down or catch people, because a farm can't replace its whole crew in two years and leave the village okay. I'm not a political man.
S2.think: I'd be out of work, because a farm with robots doesn't need a foreman. I'd be sixty with four years left on the mortgage.
S2.do: Goes to the bank about the mortgage in the first month and cuts the second car, satellite TV and family trips. Looks for any work robots aren't doing yet, like council driving or school caretaking.
S2.feel: Alarmed and awake at night with the numbers.
S2.quote: If it comes down to the house or the car, I'd walk to the farm, it's four kilometres.
S2.fieldNote: Victor would act early and sensibly, calling the bank before he falls behind. The house is the one thing he won't give up. He reluctantly floats a levy on robot sellers but insists he's not one to shout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's add a few years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan if the farmers and the government work together. I'd say it at the farm meeting, plain and calm. No sense shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd make it, just. The mortgage ends in four years, so if I hold on that long, the house is ours. Then I'd be sixty-three with nothing in the bank, which isn't nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every bit of overtime into the mortgage to clear it by 2029. I'd ask for the robot training as soon as the owner showed interest. And I'd keep an eye out for a backup job, maybe the council again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. That's better than the last one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you get done on the mortgage in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four years of overtime and no holidays, and then the bank stops writing to me, that's the deal I'd make. Ilona would say we deserve a holiday. She'd be right, but we'd go after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still ask for training on the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If the robots are coming in five years anyway, I'd rather be the man who knows them than the man who doesn't. I'd wait for the first one to work, though.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to plan if farmers and government work together. I'd say it calmly at the farm meeting.
S3.think: I think I'd just make it, because the mortgage ends in four years. Then I'd be sixty-three with no savings, which is still a worry.
S3.do: Puts all overtime into the mortgage to clear it by 2029 and skips holidays. Asks for robot training once the owner shows interest and keeps a council job as a backup.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier because he has a plan.
S3.quote: Four years of overtime and no holidays, and then the bank stops writing to me, that's the deal I'd make.
S3.fieldNote: The five-year window happens to line up with the end of his mortgage, which shapes his whole plan. He'd trade holidays for paying off the house. Steady as ever, he'd learn the robots but only once the first one has been shown to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out, no panic. I'd say that at work and to friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I think I'm mostly fine. House paid off, near the pension. It's the crew and the young men I'd think about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, clear the mortgage and then save a little each month. I'd learn whatever robots the farm brings in once they're proven. And around 2033 I'd start thinking about stopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, for other people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where are you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting on my own step, with my own front door, watching a robot cut the neighbour's hedge. That's not bad, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your sons anything about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them not to wait. One drives lorries and the other is a builder. Both could be hit, so I'd tell them to start learning the new things now, not in nine years.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to sort it out, so there's no reason to panic. I'd say that at work and to friends.
S4.think: With ten years I'm mostly fine, with the house paid off and the pension near. I'd think about the crew and the young men.
S4.do: Keeps working, clears the mortgage and then saves a little each month. Learns the farm's robots once they're proven and plans to stop work around 2033.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for other people.
S4.quote: Sitting on my own step, with my own front door, watching a robot cut the neighbour's hedge.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Victor reach his paid-off house and pension, so his calm returns. His concern turns to his sons, a lorry driver and a builder, whom he'd urge to act early. The image of his own front door shows what he values most.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the house. A robot doesn't have a mortgage, so it can work for almost nothing. I can't. What would help is some kind of mortgage break for people who lose work to machines, and a fair payment for the pickers who've given us years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The pickers. They're not in your survey, I'd guess, but they're the first to go. Someone should ask them too.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't have a mortgage, so it can work for almost nothing. I can't.
portrait: Victor Varga is a 58-year-old foreman on a vegetable and egg farm who runs a crew of seasonal pickers. He has four years left on his mortgage and almost no savings, while his wife Ilona works part-time at a pharmacy. He uses an AI translation app for safety but only adopts new things once they're proven. He's practical, not political, and his biggest concern is his house. He moves from calm in a plateau to anxious in steady change, alarmed by AGI in 2028, and steadier with five or ten years because he can clear the mortgage.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd lose his job with four years still left on the mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A mortgage break for people who lose work to machines, and a fair payment for the long-serving seasonal pickers.
